stem: Pratt's words point to the same goal as the Dawes Act of 1887. What was that goal?

stimulus.source_note: Richard Henry Pratt, 'The Advantages of Mingling Indians with Whites,' address to the National Conference of Charities and Correction, Denver, 1892. Public domain. Text verified against the Carlisle Indian School Digital Resource Center (Dickinson College) and the Minnesota Historical Society transcription.
stimulus.text:
Richard Henry Pratt, founder of the Carlisle Indian Industrial School (1879), in a speech to the National Conference of Charities and Correction, 1892 (ellipses mark omissions):

"A great general has said that the only good Indian is a dead one. In a sense, I agree with the sentiment, but only in this: that all the Indian there is in the race should be dead. Kill the Indian in him, and save the man."

options.text: To restore tribal governments and return reservation land to tribal control
options.misconception: Background: restoring tribal governments was the Indian Reorganization Act of 1934, which reversed the Dawes Act instead of sharing its goal.

options.text: To dissolve tribal life and remake Native peoples as individual, English-speaking farmers
To protect Native cultures by keeping children on their home reservations
options.misconception: Background: the boarding schools took children far from home; Pratt's Carlisle stood in Pennsylvania, far from the Plains reservations.

options.text: To prepare Native peoples for armed resistance to further settlement
options.misconception: Background: Pratt wanted assimilation, not resistance; the Ghost Dance was the spiritual resistance movement, not the schools.

rationales.A: Background: restoring tribal governments came later, in 1934, and it reversed the Dawes Act instead of sharing its goal.
rationales.B: Pratt says the 'Indian' in the child must die so the 'man' can be saved. That is the same program as allotment: end tribal life by remaking the individual.
rationales.C: Background: the schools did the opposite of protecting Native cultures. Children were taken far from home and forbidden their languages.
rationales.D: Background: nothing in Pratt's words prepares anyone to resist. His school trained children for manual labor inside white society.
rationales.general:
Picture a schoolroom in Pennsylvania where a Lakota boy is told his name, his hair, and his language must go.
1. Hear what Pratt actually promises. The 'Indian' dies so the 'man' can live.
2. Match that promise to the Dawes Act. Allotment also killed the tribe by remaking the person, one plot of land at a time.
3. Name the shared goal. Dissolve tribal life and rebuild Native peoples as individuals inside white society.
Remember: assimilation attacked the tribe through the person, whether the tool was land or a classroom.
